# Personas for outbound: what was studied

This is the research behind the linkedin-personas skill. It answers three questions: what separates an ICP from a
persona, what a persona card must hold to help write a message, and how to put each lead in one persona. Every
source is in `sources.md`; every claim with its strength is in `evidence.md`.

## Why this exists

A seller got AI messages that opened with the reader's own job title: "I saw you are Head of Asset Management." The
title had been used as the content of the message instead of as a way to find what that kind of reader cares
about. Every school below, from the design lineage to
the cold email data, points at the same repair: the title selects a card, and the card (a situation, a problem,
stakes, an objection, words) writes the message.

## The short answer

- **ICP and persona are two stages, in order.** The ICP picks the companies (observable from outside: sector,
  size, place, signals). The persona picks the people inside them and says what to say to each. Wind and Cardozo
  (1974) described exactly this as macro then micro segmentation; every outbound practitioner today draws the same
  line (Ross, Bay, the ICP versus persona pages of every sales vendor).
- **A persona is a role in a situation, not a person with a life.** Cooper split his 1995 personas by goals,
  tasks and skills. Goodwin wrote that personas "represent behavior patterns, not job descriptions". Revella
  says "pictures don't talk". In Matthews (2012), 14 practitioners reported using the role part and ignoring the
  personal detail.
- **Keep the card short, and label it a guess until replies confirm it.** Goodwin's "provisional persona" (a few
  goals, one or two traits, no narrative) is the honest form when there was no research. Chapman (2008)
  measured that a description with many attributes matches almost nobody.
- **2 to 4 personas.** No study fixes the number for messaging. A new persona earns its place only when it needs a
  different first message.
- **Write to the role's problem, not to facts about the person.** Vendor data (30MPC with Gong, 85M+ emails),
  buyer surveys (CEB 2015, Gartner 2025) and practitioners (Holland, Braun, Bay) all point the same way, with
  different strengths.

## The experts and frameworks

### Alan Cooper (origin of personas)

Cooper's own account (Cooper Journal, 2008, read from the archive): in 1983, writing a project management
program, he interviewed seven or eight colleagues and acquaintances, then play-acted one of them, "Kathy", on his
walks to decide which features mattered. He calls it "primitive". In 1995, for the Sagent project, he
interviewed about six clients and found three groups "clearly differentiated by their goals, tasks, and skill
levels": Chuck, Cynthia and Rob, one interface each. He formalised personas because, as a consultant, he "had to
persuade" clients. Two consequences for us: personas were built to make a choice and to align people, not to
describe a market; and the axes were goals and behaviour, never demographics. His 1999 book even has a section
titled "It's a User Persona, Not a Buyer Persona" (title read, body not): the buyer persona is a later borrowing.

Kim Goodwin, in the same consultancy, wrote the method down (2001, 2002): interview a dozen people, list
behavioural variables, cluster on six to eight of them; personas are not job titles in either direction; if
every detail cannot be tied back to data it is "a creative writing project"; with little research, write
"provisional personas" and say they are guesses. Her line on detail is the one to keep: a precise description
claims you observed that precision.

### Pruitt and Grudin (Microsoft, 2003)

The industrial method: start from market segmentation data, choose 3 to 6 segments by size and strategy, build
a foundation document where every statement carries a footnote, add one anti-persona (who you are not designing
for), and score features per persona in a weighted matrix. They tried "organization archetypes" for whole
companies (an ICP inside the persona literature) and wrote "the verdict is still out". And: "We have not tried
to formally measure the impact of our Personas." The data requirement entered the tradition here, against
Cooper by name.

### Chapman and the evidence against

Chapman and Milham (2006): a persona cannot be falsified, so it cannot be validated. Chapman et al. (2008), six
real survey datasets: at nine or more attributes the best 1% of descriptions match no one in five of six
datasets. They say plainly this does not measure whether personas are useful. What carries over: every attribute
added to a card narrows who it describes, so a card should hold the few things that change the message.

The usage studies (Matthews 2012, Friess 2012, Ronkko 2005) agree that teams invoke personas to communicate and
justify, rarely while deciding. Nielsen and Hansen (2014) found the opposite in Danish companies by self-report.
Salminen and Jansen's group, the largest persona research programme, wrote in 2023 that the value of personas
for marketing "has not been systematically studied". Their reviews of AI-made personas (2025) found
demographics in almost all of them, no evaluation in about half the studies, and a circularity risk when the
same model writes and judges. That is a direct warning for a skill where Claude drafts the cards: the user must
correct them, and replies must judge them.

### Adele Revella and the Buyer Persona Institute

Read in full (The Buyer Persona Manifesto, 2016). Revella keeps a short profile (who the person is) but puts the
value in the **5 Rings of Buying Insight**, which "reveal the buying decision you need to influence":

1. **Priority initiatives**: what makes some buyers invest time, budget or political capital now, while others
   stay with the status quo. She warns not to confuse this with pain points reverse engineered from your
   product's capabilities.
2. **Success factors**: the operational or personal results they expect, written from their side ("reduce
   business risk", not "cut costs").
3. **Perceived barriers**: "the bad news insight", why they will not buy from you: internal resistance, scars
   from a past project, a perception of your company.
4. **Buyer's journey**: who is involved and how the decision unfolds; often the top of the hierarchy has less
   clout than vendors assume.
5. **Decision criteria**: the three to five capabilities that matter and what the buyer means by them.

Her method: six to ten interviews with people who decided "in the past several months", open questions ("What
happened on the day you decided to look for a solution like this?"), quote the buyer's own words. She claims
insight-based personas need "half as many" as demographic ones, with no data shown.

For a seller with no interviews, the card adapts the rings: ring 1 becomes the trigger and priority, ring 2 the
goal, ring 3 the objections, rings 4 and 5 shrink to "who else decides" and "what they will judge you on". The
seller's own past conversations, won deals and lost deals stand in for interviews.

The "buyer persona" term itself is Tony Zambito's (2002): research-based archetypes of what buyers try to
accomplish, how they think and how they buy. ITSMA (2017) adds a useful warning: profiles built from second-hand
data are "role-based profiles", heavy on demographics and pain points, light on buying behaviour. What Claude can
write from a user's knowledge and public profiles is a role-based profile; the skill should call it a card and
treat it as a hypothesis.

### Jobs to be done (Christensen, Moesta, Klement, Ulwick)

Christensen (Competing Against Luck, 2016): people "hire" a product to make progress in a circumstance. Bob
Moesta and Chris Spiek built the interview method and the **four forces**: push of the current situation, pull of
the new solution, anxiety about the new, habit of the present. A switch happens when push and pull beat anxiety
and habit. Moesta and Greg Engle's Demand-Side Sales 101 (2020) applies it to selling: help the buyer make
progress, do not push. Alan Klement and Intercom's **job stories** ("When ..., I want to ..., so I can ...") put the
situation first and drop the demographic persona. Ulwick's quantified version (Outcome-Driven Innovation) needs a
survey of 50 to 150 outcome statements and is out of reach for a seller; its "86% success rate" is 18 of 21
client launches, self-rated.

What carries over: a first message can name the push (the situation) and lower the anxiety (the risk). It cannot
create pull in one paragraph or break habit. Romaniuk (2022, Ehrenberg-Bass with the LinkedIn B2B Institute)
adds that every B2B reader has two jobs: the company's, and their own (credit, promotion, not being blamed). A
card holds both.

### Eugene Schwartz, stages of awareness

Breakthrough Advertising (1966): the headline must start from what the reader already knows, because the same
message cannot serve every state of awareness. The five labels everyone uses (unaware, problem aware, solution
aware, product aware, most aware) are a modern shorthand: no page reached quotes Schwartz's own wording, and one
copywriter says he compiled the scale himself. Use the idea, not a quote. For cold outbound almost every reader
is unaware or problem aware: they do not know the sender, and many do not name the problem. So a first message
names a situation they recognise, not a product; a card records the likely stage per persona because it decides
whether the message opens on the problem or on the result.

### Challenger, CEB and Gartner (buying groups)

The Challenger Sale (Dixon and Adamson, 2011) taught "tailor" to each stakeholder. The Challenger Customer (2015)
then reported, from CEB's survey, that positioning value to one individual stakeholder was associated with -4% in
the likelihood of a high-quality sale and "collective learning" with +20%. Gartner (2025, 632 buyers) found that
individual-level relevance hurts consensus and group-level relevance makes a high-quality deal three times more
likely. Both are self-reported, measured inside active purchases, not at a cold first touch, and relative figures
with no base. The sign is consistent: the message should carry what the reader can take to their team, not
flattery. Their seven stakeholder types (Go-Getter, Teacher, Skeptic, Friend, Guide, Climber, Blocker) are
behaviour seen in a deal, not on a profile, so they cannot sort leads.

The buying-group sizes in circulation (4.8 to 23) depend on how they were counted; there is no constant. The
card asks the question instead: who else decides, who uses it, who can block it.

### ICP against persona, as outbound practitioners define it

- **Aaron Ross** (Predictable Revenue, 2011): a written ICP before any prospecting (company type, size, triggers,
  target titles). Summaries only.
- **Winning by Design**, SPICED (Situation, Pain, Impact, Critical Event, Decision): a discovery frame, but its
  "critical event" (a dated reason it must happen now) is the best name for a trigger.
- **Pavilion** and the sales vendor literature: the ICP says where to go, the persona who to talk to and what to
  say. No Pavilion primary was found; the distinction is consensus, not a finding.
- **Jason Bay** (Outbound Squad): the core of a cold email is to say you solve a problem and ask whether they have
  it; persona work is the planning step. Video and podcast pages only.
- **Josh Braun**: lead with a question that surfaces a problem the reader has not named; no pitch first.
- **Becc Holland**: personalisation is about the person, relevance is about the role and context; with no real
  personal premise, stay relevant to the role.
- **30MPC with Gong** (85M+ cold emails, read): executives do not care about their alma mater; reference business
  problems, not personal fun facts; pitch words and "we" language lower replies. Vendor data with no method
  section: trust the direction, not the numbers.

### Empathy map (Dave Gray, XPLANE)

Made at XPLANE, popularised in Gamestorming (2010), updated in 2017 to start from a goal ("WHO are we
empathizing with? What do they need to DO?") and then what they see, say, do, hear, think and feel, with pains
and gains. Useful as a set of prompts when the user knows the people well; on its own it produces an attribute
pile. The skill keeps two of its prompts: what they say (their words) and what they need to do.

### Value Proposition Canvas (Strategyzer)

Osterwalder, Pigneur, Bernarda and Smith (2014): a customer profile of jobs, pains and gains, matched against a
value map of products, pain relievers and gain creators. Strategyzer's own line, "Fit is a claim until customers
confirm it", is the right status for a card. The skill uses the pain to proof link: each pain on a card should
point to one proof the seller can show.

### Pain and objection mapping

Revella's perceived barriers and Moesta's anxiety and habit are the two sources for objections. The useful
split for a card: "not now" (habit, no trigger), "not you" (a perception of the seller), "not my call" (someone
else decides), "we tried" (scars). Each needs a different line in a follow-up, so the card names the likely one.

### Addressing the reader formally or informally

No study tests formal against informal address on B2B reply rates. The perception studies are mixed: informal
fits warm brands and formal fits competent ones (Leung et al. 2023); in German sales talk du gave no advantage and
Sie, where it differed, was rated better (Kretzenbacher and Hensel-Boerner 2024); German and French participants
preferred a formal recruiter. A first message to a stranger in French, German, Italian, Spanish or Dutch is
therefore safer formal, unless the persona's world plainly speaks informally (start-up founders, tech, a shared
community), and then mirror the reader's reply. The card records the choice per persona.

### Classifying a lead into one persona

A model sorts job titles into broad functions well (about 92.6% on 500 checked titles in one study), but labels
built from titles alone are often wrong (63% in a resume dataset), and Goodwin's rule says a title cannot settle a
persona anyway. The skill sorts on three observable things (title and seniority, company type, what the person
writes and reacts to), gives one line of why, and marks "unsure" rather than forcing a fit. BeReach's on-demand
fit check (`bereach_check_fit`) does the same for a whole list and returns the persona each person reads as, with
one line of why; it hides and blocks nobody.


## Limits of this work

Books read only through tables of contents or summaries: Cooper 1999, Revella 2015, Christensen 2016, Moesta and
Engle 2020, Osterwalder 2014, Schwartz 1966, Ross 2011, Dixon and Adamson 2011. Several peer-reviewed papers were
reached at the abstract only (Friess, Leung et al., Kretzenbacher and Hensel-Boerner). No study anywhere measures
whether persona cards improve cold outreach replies; the skill's own loop (reply rate per persona) is the only
measurement it will get.
